1. How to start the session

Opening speech – Talk directly to students

"Good morning, everyone!

Welcome to our Web Development workshop!

Before we start, I want to ask you something.

How many of you have used Google today?

How many of you have opened Instagram, YouTube, Amazon, or your college website?

Almost everyone, right?

Now, here is my question.

Have you ever wondered what actually happens when you type www.google.com in your browser and press Enter?

How does Google know what page to show you?

Where is that website actually stored?

How does your browser understand the colours, images, buttons, and text?

And how can you create your own website?

That is exactly what we are going to learn!

I don't want you to sit here for four days and simply listen to me explaining definitions.

I want you to create things.

You will write code, break code, correct code, experiment with designs, compete with your friends, and build your own websites.

'Yes! I created this website myself!'

So, let's begin!"

2. Internet Fundamentals

Topic 1: Internet vs World Wide Web

Explain to students:

"Let's start with a very basic question.

Are the Internet and the World Wide Web the same thing?

Many people use these two terms interchangeably, but technically, they are different.

The Internet is a massive network of interconnected computers and devices across the world.

The World Wide Web, commonly called the Web, is a service that operates using the Internet.

Let me give you an example.

Think of the Internet as a road network.

The Web is like the collection of shops, offices, and buildings that you can visit using those roads.

The Internet provides the connection, while the Web provides websites and webpages that we access through that connection.

So remember:

  • Internet = Global network infrastructure.

  • Web = Collection of interconnected webpages and websites.

Now, can you name three things that use the Internet but are not necessarily websites?"

Expected student answers:

  • WhatsApp messages

  • Online gaming

  • Email applications

  • Video calls

  • File transfers

"Excellent! This is why the Internet is much bigger than just websites."

Fun activity 1: Internet or Web?

Tell students:

"I'm going to mention some applications and activities. You tell me whether they primarily represent a Web service or another Internet-based service."

Example

Answer

Opening Google Chrome and visiting Wikipedia

Web

Sending a WhatsApp message

Internet-based messaging

Watching a webpage on YouTube

Web

Playing an online multiplayer game

Internet-based gaming

Accessing an online shopping website

Web

Make this a quick team competition. Give one point for each correct answer.

Topic 2: How the Internet works

uploadcare.com

Direct teaching speech:

"Now let's understand something very important: how your browser communicates with a website.

Imagine that you want to visit our college website.

You open Chrome and enter the website address.

Your browser sends a request through the Internet to a computer called a web server.

The web server receives your request, finds the required webpage, and sends the response back.

Your browser then displays the webpage.

This is called the Client-Server Model.

There are two important participants:

  1. Client – The device or application requesting information. For example, your browser.

  2. Server – The computer that stores or processes website resources and sends responses.

Let's understand this with a simple restaurant example.

You are the customer. You are the client.

You place an order.

The kitchen receives the order and prepares your food. The kitchen is acting like the server.

The food comes back to you. That is the response.

Similarly, your browser requests a webpage and the server responds with the required content."

Quick student activity: Become the Internet!

"Let's do something interesting.

I need three volunteers.

  • Student 1: You are the browser.

  • Student 2: You are the Internet.

  • Student 3: You are the web server.

The browser student should request a webpage.

The Internet student should carry the request to the server.

The server should respond with the webpage.

Now reverse the roles!

See? You have just demonstrated the client-server model!"

Topic 3: LAN, WAN, IP Address, DNS and URL

LAN – Local Area Network

"LAN means Local Area Network.

Imagine all the computers in your computer laboratory are connected to the same network.

They can communicate with each other through that network.

That is an example of a LAN."

WAN – Wide Area Network

"WAN means Wide Area Network.

It connects networks across larger geographical areas.

The Internet is the largest and most familiar example of a global interconnected network."

Concept

Explain it like this

IP Address

A numerical address used to identify a device on an IP network.

DNS

The system that translates domain names into IP addresses.

Domain Name

The human-readable name of a website.

URL

The complete address of a particular online resource.

Web Server

A system that serves website content.

Hosting

A service that makes website files available online.

Demonstration 1: Let students discover their IP address

Tell students:

"Now we are going to use our computers to discover networking information.

Don't just write down the definition of an IP address. Let's actually see one!"

Ask students to open Command Prompt on Windows.

Type:

Bash
ipconfig

Explain:

  • ipconfig – Displays Windows network configuration information.

  • Look for IPv4 Address – This is the device's local IPv4 address for that network interface.

  • Look for Default Gateway – This is generally the address of the router through which the device reaches other networks.

Next, type:

Bash
ping google.com

Explain:

  • ping – Tests whether a destination responds to network echo requests.

  • google.com – The destination hostname.

  • The output may show response times and packet statistics.

Tell students:

"Notice something interesting.

We typed a website name, but our computer communicated using network addressing.

Something must translate the website name into an IP address.

That something is DNS!"

Demonstration 2: See DNS in action

Type:

Bash
nslookup google.com

Explain:

  • nslookup – Queries the DNS system.

  • google.com – The domain name we want to resolve.

  • Address – Displays the DNS server or resolved IP address, depending on the section of output.

Ask:

"Why do we use Google.com instead of remembering a long numerical IP address?"

Expected answer: Domain names are easier for humans to remember.

Topic 4: URL, HTTP and HTTPS

newsletter.techworld-with-milan.com

Tell students:

"Let's look at a URL.

For example:

https://www.example.com/students/profile

A URL contains different parts.

  • https – Protocol.

  • www.example.com – Hostname.

  • /students/profile – Path.

Now let's understand HTTP and HTTPS.

HTTP stands for Hypertext Transfer Protocol.

It is used for communication between web clients and servers.

HTTPS is HTTP secured using encryption through TLS.

When you access a website using HTTPS, the communication is protected in transit against many forms of interception and tampering.

That is why we prefer HTTPS for websites, especially websites that handle login credentials or personal information."

Fun activity 2: Find the secure website

"Open your browser.

Visit two websites that you commonly use.

Look at the address bar.

Can you identify HTTPS?

Now tell me: Does HTTPS mean that a website is automatically trustworthy?

No!

HTTPS protects the connection, but it does not guarantee that the website itself is honest or safe."

This is a useful cybersecurity lesson too!

Topic 5: How a website loads – Complete request-response flow

Draw this on the board:

User enters a URL

Browser / Client

DNS lookup and request preparation

Internet / Network

Request travels to the server

Web Server

Processes the request and sends a response

Browser displays the webpage

"Whenever you visit a website, a series of communication steps takes place.

Your browser prepares a request, DNS helps resolve the domain name, the browser establishes a connection, and the server responds with the requested resources.

The browser then processes HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images, and other resources to display the page.

This is the foundation of web development.

And now that you understand how websites communicate, let's learn how to create one!"

3. HTML – Building the Structure of a Website

Topic 1: What is HTML?

Direct teaching speech:

"Now we are entering the actual web development part!

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.

HTML is used to structure the content of webpages.

Imagine building a house.

Before painting the walls or decorating the rooms, we need the basic structure.

Similarly, before styling a website, we need to create its structure.

HTML gives us:

  • Headings

  • Paragraphs

  • Images

  • Links

  • Lists

  • Tables

  • Forms

  • Sections

  • Navigation areas

One important thing: HTML is a markup language, not a programming language.

Why?

Because HTML defines the structure and meaning of content rather than providing general-purpose programming logic."

Topic 2: First live coding session

Live coding – Practical 1

Your instruction to students:

"Everyone, open your computer.

We are going to create our first webpage.

You don't need to memorise anything right now. Watch what I type, understand what each line does, and then type it yourself."

Step 1: Set up the project

Ask students to:

  1. Create a folder called Day1_WebWorkshop.

  2. Open Visual Studio Code.

  3. Open this folder in VS Code.

  4. Create a file called index.html.

Explain:

"HTML files normally use the .html extension. Our main webpage will be named index.html."

Step 2: Type the first HTML program

Type this code live. The comments alongside each line are your teaching prompts.

HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<!-- Tell the browser that this is an HTML5 document -->

<html lang="en">
<!-- Start the HTML document and declare its language -->

<head>
    <!-- The head contains page information and settings -->

    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <!-- Support standard Unicode characters -->

    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <!-- Make the page adapt to mobile screen widths -->

    <title>My First Website</title>
    <!-- Set the title displayed in the browser tab -->

</head>
<!-- Close the head section -->

<body>
    <!-- All visible webpage content goes inside body -->

    <h1>Welcome to Web Development!</h1>
    <!-- Display the main heading -->

    <p>Hello everyone! This is my first webpage.</p>
    <!-- Display a paragraph -->

</body>
<!-- Close the body section -->

</html>
<!-- Close the HTML document -->

Explain the code line by line

"Let's understand what we have just written.

DOCTYPE html tells the browser that we are using HTML5.

The html tag is the root element of our webpage.

The head section contains information about our page, such as the title and metadata.

The meta charset tag tells the browser which character encoding to use.

The viewport meta tag helps the page adapt to different screen widths.

The title tag defines the title displayed in the browser tab.

The body tag contains the content that users actually see.

The h1 tag creates our main heading.

The p tag creates a paragraph.

Congratulations! You have just created your first webpage!"

Step 3: View the webpage

"Now save your file.

Open the HTML file in your browser.

Look at the result!

You have created a webpage using HTML.

Now let's experiment.

Change the heading.

Change the paragraph.

Add your name.

Save the file and refresh your browser.

See how the webpage changes immediately?"

Topic 3: HTML elements, tags and attributes

"Now let's understand three important words.

A tag is the markup written inside angle brackets.

An element is generally the complete structure, including the opening tag, content and closing tag.

An attribute provides additional information about an element."

Example:

HTML
<a href="https://www.google.com">Visit Google</a>

Explain:

  • <a> – Opening anchor tag.

  • href – Attribute specifying the destination.

  • https://www.google.com – Attribute value.

  • Visit Google – Visible link text.

  • </a> – Closing anchor tag.

Student experiment

"Change the link to your favourite website.

Then open your webpage and click the link.

You have now created a clickable hyperlink!"

6. Semantic HTML – Give Meaning to Your Website

hartenfeller.dev

Explain to students:

"Until now, we have used elements such as headings, paragraphs and images.

Now let's understand semantic HTML.

Semantic means meaningful.

Semantic HTML elements describe the purpose of different parts of a webpage.

For example:

  • header – Introductory content or page header.

  • nav – Navigation links.

  • main – Main content of the webpage.

  • section – A thematic section.

  • article – Independent, self-contained content.

  • aside – Related or supplementary content.

  • footer – Footer information.

Why is this important?

Because it makes webpages easier to understand, maintain, navigate using assistive technologies, and structure for search engines."

Live coding – Semantic webpage

HTML

<!DOCTYPE html>
<!-- Declare HTML5 -->

<html lang="en">
<!-- Start the document -->

<head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <!-- Set character encoding -->

    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">
    <!-- Enable responsive viewport behaviour -->

    <title>My College</title>
    <!-- Set browser tab title -->

</head>

<body>
<!-- Start visible content -->

    <header>
    <!-- Create the page header -->

        <h1>ABC College</h1>
        <!-- Display college name -->

        <p>Learning Today, Leading Tomorrow</p>
        <!-- Display a tagline -->

    </header>

    <nav>
    <!-- Create navigation area -->

        <a href="#home">Home</a>
        <!-- Link to home section -->

        <a href="#about">About</a>
        <!-- Link to about section -->

        <a href="#courses">Courses</a>
        <!-- Link to courses section -->

        <a href="#contact">Contact</a>
        <!-- Link to contact section -->

    </nav>

    <main>
    <!-- Start the primary page content -->

        <section id="home">
        <!-- Create home section -->

            <h2>Welcome to ABC College</h2>
            <!-- Section heading -->

            <p>Welcome to our college website.</p>
            <!-- Section description -->

        </section>

        <section id="about">
        <!-- Create about section -->

            <h2>About Us</h2>

            <p>We provide quality education.</p>

        </section>

        <section id="courses">
        <!-- Create courses section -->

            <h2>Our Courses</h2>

            <ul>
                <li>BCA</li>
                <li>BBA</li>
                <li>BSc</li>
            </ul>

        </section>

        <section id="contact">
        <!-- Create contact section -->

            <h2>Contact Us</h2>

            <p>Email: abc@example.com</p>

        </section>

    </main>

    <footer>
    <!-- Create footer -->

        <p>&copy; 2026 ABC College. All rights reserved.</p>
        <!-- Display copyright information -->

    </footer>

</body>
</html>
<!-- Close the document -->

"Look at what we have created.

We now have a properly structured webpage.

Notice that when I click About, the browser moves to the About section.

That happens because our navigation link points to the section's ID.

This is one of the simplest ways to create navigation within a webpage."

7. CSS – Make Your Website Beautiful

Direct teaching speech:

"Now, we have created the structure of our website.

But does it look attractive?

Not particularly!

This is where CSS comes in.

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.

HTML creates the structure, while CSS controls how that structure looks.

Imagine HTML as the skeleton of a human body and CSS as the appearance, clothing and presentation.

CSS allows us to control:

  • Colours

  • Fonts

  • Backgrounds

  • Borders

  • Spacing

  • Layouts

  • Animations

  • Responsive designs

Let's make our website beautiful!"

Topic 1: Three ways of using CSS

"CSS can be applied in three main ways."

1. Inline CSS

HTML
<h1 style="color: red;">Hello Students</h1>
<!-- Apply CSS directly to this HTML element -->

"Here, we are writing the CSS inside the HTML element using the style attribute."

2. Internal CSS

HTML
<head>
    <style>
        /* Start the internal CSS section */

        h1 {
            color: blue;
        }
        /* Make all h1 headings blue */

    </style>
</head>

"Here, the CSS is written inside the style tag in the HTML document."

3. External CSS

"Now, this is the approach we will mainly use in our workshop.

We will create a separate CSS file and connect it to our HTML document.

Why?

Because it keeps our HTML and CSS separate and makes our project easier to maintain."

Create a file called style.css.

Connect it inside the HTML head:

HTML
<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">
<!-- Connect the external stylesheet to the HTML document -->

Topic 2: CSS selectors

Explain:

"Before styling an element, we need to tell CSS which element we want to style.

This is done using selectors."

CSS

/* Element selector: select all paragraph elements */
p {
    color: blue;
}

/* Class selector: select elements with class highlight */
.highlight {
    background-color: yellow;
}

/* ID selector: select the element with ID heading */
#heading {
    color: red;
}

/* Universal selector: select every element */
* {
    margin: 0;
    padding: 0;
}

/* Group selector: select multiple elements together */
h1, h2, h3 {
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
}

Tell students:

"Notice the difference.

An element selector uses the element name.

A class selector starts with a dot.

An ID selector starts with a hash symbol.

A class can be reused on multiple elements, while an ID should uniquely identify one element within a page."

Mini challenge

"Create three paragraphs.

Give one paragraph the class highlight.

Give another paragraph the ID special.

Use CSS to make all three look different."

8. CSS Box Model – One of the Most Important Concepts

euron.one

Direct teaching speech:

"Now we are going to understand one of the most important concepts in CSS: the Box Model.

Every HTML element is treated as a rectangular box for layout purposes.

The box model has four main parts:

  1. Content

  2. Padding

  3. Border

  4. Margin

Let me explain with an example.

Imagine that you have a gift box.

The actual gift is the content.

The protective material around it is padding.

The outer covering is the border.

The space between this gift box and another box is margin.

Let's see this practically."

Live coding

CSS

/* Select the box */
.box {

    width: 200px;
    /* Set content width to 200 pixels */

    padding: 20px;
    /* Add 20 pixels of internal spacing */

    border: 5px solid black;
    /* Add a 5 pixel solid border */

    margin: 30px;
    /* Add 30 pixels of external spacing */

    background-color: lightblue;
    /* Set background colour */

}

Explain:

"Here, the content width is 200 pixels.

We add 40 pixels of horizontal padding and 10 pixels of horizontal border.

Therefore, the total width is 250 pixels, excluding margins.

If we include the left and right margins, the overall occupied horizontal space is 310 pixels."

Introduce:

CSS
* {
    box-sizing: border-box;
}

"With border-box, the declared width includes the content, padding and border.

This makes layout calculations much easier."

10. CSS Flexbox – Build a Real Navigation Bar

scrimba.com

Direct teaching speech:

"Imagine that you want to display a website logo on the left side and navigation links on the right side.

You could try using spaces or manually adjusting margins.

But that is not the professional approach.

CSS Flexbox helps us arrange elements efficiently in a row or column.

Let's build a navigation bar."

Live coding

CSS

/* Select the navigation container */
.navbar {

    display: flex;
    /* Enable Flexbox layout */

    justify-content: space-between;
    /* Place items at opposite ends */

    align-items: center;
    /* Vertically align items */

    background-color: #172554;
    /* Set dark blue background */

    padding: 20px;
    /* Add internal spacing */

}

/* Select the navigation links */
.navbar a {

    color: white;
    /* Make link text white */

    text-decoration: none;
    /* Remove underline */

    margin: 10px;
    /* Add spacing around links */

}

Explain the three important properties:

  • display: flex – Enables Flexbox.

  • justify-content – Controls alignment along the main axis.

  • align-items – Controls alignment along the cross axis.

"Now change space-between to center.

What happens?

Change it to space-around.

What happens now?

I want you to experiment rather than memorise the property names."

11. Responsive Web Design – Make Websites Work on Mobile

Tell students:

"Think about the devices you use.

Some of you are using laptops.

Some are using smartphones.

Some websites look excellent on a laptop but terrible on a mobile screen.

Why?

Because they are not properly responsive.

Responsive Web Design means designing webpages so that they adapt to different screen sizes and devices.

CSS provides media queries to help us achieve this."

Live coding – Media Query

CSS

/* Default styles for larger screens */
.container {

    width: 80%;
    /* Use 80 percent of the available width */

    margin: auto;
    /* Centre the container */

}

/* Apply these styles when screen width is 600px or less */
@media (max-width: 600px) {

    .container {

        width: 95%;
        /* Use almost the full mobile screen width */

    }

    h1 {

        font-size: 24px;
        /* Reduce heading size on smaller screens */

    }

    .navbar {

        flex-direction: column;
        /* Arrange navigation items vertically */

    }

}

Live demonstration

"Now open your webpage.

Make the browser window smaller.

Observe how the layout changes.

You can also press F12 to open Developer Tools.

Click the device toolbar and select a mobile device.

Congratulations! You have just tested responsive web design."

Major hands-on project

  2. A welcome section.

  3. An about section.

I want everyone to build this website with me.

Step 3: Create style.css

Now tell students:

"Your HTML is ready.

But it looks like a basic document.

Let's use CSS to turn it into a proper event website."

CSS

/* Apply box sizing consistently to all elements */
* {
    box-sizing: border-box;
    margin: 0;
    /* Remove default outer spacing */
    padding: 0;
    /* Remove default inner spacing */
}

/* Style the entire webpage */
body {
    font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
    /* Set the website font */

    background-color: #f1f5f9;
    /* Set a light background */

    color: #1e293b;
    /* Set default text colour */

    line-height: 1.6;
    /* Improve text readability */
}

/* Style the header */
header {
    background-color: #172554;
    /* Set dark blue background */

    color: white;
    /* Set text colour */

    padding: 20px;
    /* Add internal spacing */

    display: flex;
    /* Enable Flexbox */

    justify-content: space-between;
    /* Separate title and navigation */

    align-items: center;
    /* Vertically align content */
}

/* Style navigation links */
nav a {
    color: white;
    /* Make links white */

    text-decoration: none;
    /* Remove underlines */

    margin: 10px;
    /* Add space between links */
}

/* Style the welcome section */
.hero {
    background: linear-gradient(135deg, #1e3a8a, #7c3aed);
    /* Add a gradient background */

    color: white;
    /* Make text white */

    text-align: center;
    /* Centre the content */

    padding: 100px 20px;
    /* Add space around the content */
}

/* Style section headings */
section h2 {
    text-align: center;
    /* Centre the heading */

    margin-bottom: 20px;
    /* Add space below the heading */
}

/* Style general sections */
section {
    padding: 50px 8%;
    /* Add internal spacing */
}

/* Style the event container */
.event-container {
    display: flex;
    /* Enable Flexbox */

    justify-content: center;
    /* Centre the event cards */

    gap: 20px;
    /* Add space between cards */

    flex-wrap: wrap;
    /* Allow cards to move to another row */
}

/* Style individual event cards */
.card {
    background-color: white;
    /* Set card background */

    padding: 25px;
    /* Add internal spacing */

    border-radius: 12px;
    /* Round card corners */

    width: 250px;
    /* Set card width */

    text-align: center;
    /* Centre card content */

    box-shadow: 0 4px 10px rgba(0,0,0,0.1);
    /* Add a subtle shadow */
}

/* Style registration form */
form {
    max-width: 450px;
    /* Limit form width */

    margin: auto;
    /* Centre the form */

    display: flex;
    /* Enable Flexbox */

    flex-direction: column;
    /* Arrange form fields vertically */

    gap: 12px;
    /* Add space between form elements */
}

/* Style form inputs and dropdown */
input, select {
    padding: 12px;
    /* Add internal spacing */

    border: 1px solid #cbd5e1;
    /* Add a light border */

    border-radius: 6px;
    /* Round the corners */
}

/* Style buttons */
button, .btn {
    background-color: #2563eb;
    /* Set blue background */

    color: white;
    /* Set white text */

    padding: 12px 20px;
    /* Add button spacing */

    border: none;
    /* Remove default border */

    border-radius: 6px;
    /* Round button corners */

    cursor: pointer;
    /* Display pointer on hover */

    text-decoration: none;
    /* Remove link underline */

}

/* Add a hover effect */
button:hover, .btn:hover {
    background-color: #1d4ed8;
    /* Change background on hover */
}

/* Style the footer */
footer {
    background-color: #172554;
    /* Set dark background */

    color: white;
    /* Set footer text colour */

    text-align: center;
    /* Centre footer text */

    padding: 20px;
    /* Add internal spacing */
}

/* Responsive styles for mobile screens */
@media (max-width: 600px) {

    header {
        flex-direction: column;
        /* Stack header content vertically */

        gap: 15px;
        /* Add spacing between elements */
    }

    nav {
        display: flex;
        /* Enable Flexbox for navigation */

        flex-wrap: wrap;
        /* Allow links to wrap */

        justify-content: center;
        /* Centre navigation links */
    }

    .hero {
        padding: 60px 15px;
        /* Reduce hero spacing on mobile */
    }

    section {
        padding: 35px 15px;
        /* Reduce section spacing */
    }

    .card {
        width: 100%;
        /* Make cards fill the available width */
    }
}

13. Make the Practical More Fun – Classroom Challenges

I strongly recommend using these activities between the coding demonstrations. This prevents students from becoming passive listeners.

Challenge 1 – Web Detective

5–10 minutes

"Open any website. Identify its header, navigation bar, main content, images, buttons and footer. Tell me which HTML elements could be used to build those sections."

Challenge 2 – Debugging Battle

10 minutes

"I am going to give you a webpage with five mistakes. Work with your partner and identify all five errors. The first team to fix everything wins."

Challenge 3 – Design Your Own College Website

15 minutes

"Each group must design a homepage for our college. You can choose the colours, fonts, layout and sections. I want creativity, not copied designs."

Challenge 4 – 10-Minute Website Challenge

10 minutes

"Create a webpage containing your name, photograph, short introduction, three skills and a contact link. Make it look attractive using CSS."

Challenge 5 – Inspect and Experiment

10 minutes

"Open a website, right-click and select Inspect. Find an HTML heading and change its text or CSS colour temporarily. Notice what happens. You are now experimenting with the browser's Developer Tools!"

Use these as a quick oral quiz at the end of the session.

2. Which system translates domain names into IP addresses?

4. Which HTML element creates a hyperlink?

6. What does padding control in CSS?

7. Which CSS property enables Flexbox?

8. Which HTML element creates a dropdown?

9. Which element represents the main content of a webpage?

15. Final Wrap-Up – Closing Speech

Speak directly to students:

"Excellent work, everyone!

Let's take a moment to understand what we have achieved today.

This morning, many of you might have thought that creating a website required advanced programming knowledge.

But look at what you have created!

You learned how the Internet works.

You understood IP addresses, DNS, domains, HTTP and HTTPS.

You created your first HTML webpage.

You added headings, paragraphs, images, links, lists and tables.

You created a registration form.

You understood semantic HTML.

You used CSS to add colours, backgrounds, borders, spacing and typography.

You worked with the CSS Box Model.

You created layouts using Flexbox.

You also made your webpage responsive.

And finally, you built your own College TechFest website!

But remember something important.

Web development is not about memorising hundreds of HTML tags or CSS properties.

It is about understanding how to solve problems and building something useful.

If your code does not work, don't panic.

Find the mistake.

Understand why it happened.

Correct it.

That is how developers learn.

Tomorrow, we will continue developing our skills and make our websites even more interactive.

Before we finish, I want each of you to open the website you created today and show it to the person sitting next to you.

Be proud of what you have built.

Thank you, everyone!"

3. Commands that differ between Mac and Windows

Activity A: Check the computer's IP address

Tell students:

"Let's inspect the network configuration of our computers. I will type the command on my Mac, and you will type the equivalent command on Windows."

Your Mac — Terminal

Bash
ifconfig

To find the IP address of the Wi-Fi interface, you can also use:

Bash

Note: en0 is commonly Wi-Fi on Macs, but the interface name can vary.

Students' Windows — Command Prompt

bat
ipconfig

Ask students to look for IPv4 Address under their active Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter.

What to say:

"Notice that the commands are different, but we are trying to find similar information. On Windows, ipconfig displays the network configuration. On macOS, we commonly use ifconfig or ipconfig getifaddr en0 to inspect network information."

Activity B: Test the Internet connection

Good news: this command works on both operating systems!

Bash
ping google.com

Explain:

  • ping — Sends network echo requests to test connectivity.

  • google.com — The destination hostname.

  • The response may display the resolved IP address and response time.

Important difference: On macOS, ping normally continues until you stop it with Control + C. On Windows, ping normally sends four requests and stops automatically.

Tell students:

"If your Mac keeps displaying results, press Control + C to stop the command. On Windows, the command normally finishes automatically after four requests."

Activity C: Find the DNS information

This command also works on both:

Bash
nslookup google.com

Explain:

"nslookup queries DNS information for the domain. We can use it on both Mac and Windows, so you can follow exactly what I demonstrate."

Activity D: Open the project folder in Visual Studio Code

If VS Code is installed and its code command is available in the terminal:

Mac and Windows:

Bash

Explain:

"code launches Visual Studio Code, and the dot means the current directory. If you see an error, don't worry; we can open the folder using the File menu in VS Code instead."

On Windows, students can also open VS Code from the Start menu and choose File → Open Folder. On Mac, use File → Open Folder as well.
